headline: A Locked Door in Studio C
standfirst: In 1970 Joni Mitchell stepped off the stage, packed a dulcimer and went looking for somewhere quieter. What she brought back to Hollywood was ten songs with almost nothing between the singer and the listener.

sections.heading: A year away
paragraphs: By the spring of 1970 Joni Mitchell had travelled a long way in a short time. Born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alberta, in November 1943, she grew up mostly in Saskatoon, came through polio at the age of nine, and taught herself guitar from a Pete Seeger songbook. The weakness the illness left in her left hand is one reason she reached for the open tunings that became her signature. She studied art in Calgary, sang in the coffeehouses of Toronto’s Yorkville, married the folk singer Chuck Mitchell in 1965 and moved with him to Detroit, and when the marriage ended she carried on alone to New York.

For a while her songs were better known than she was. Judy Collins took “Both Sides Now” into the American top ten, and Tom Rush recorded “Urge for Going”. David Crosby saw her play in Florida in 1967 and helped bring her to Reprise Records, which released *Song to a Seagull* in March 1968. *Clouds* followed in 1969 and won a Grammy for Best Folk Performance. *Ladies of the Canyon*, in April 1970, became her first gold record and sent “Big Yellow Taxi” and “Woodstock” out into the world. That year the readers of *Melody Maker* voted her the top female singer anywhere.

Success had a sharper edge than the polls suggested. In August 1970 she faced a restless, hostile crowd at the Isle of Wight Festival, a bruising experience that her biographer Brian Hinton treats as a turning point. Her relationship with Graham Nash was over. She decided to take a year off from touring to write and paint, and she went travelling. The songs she gathered on the way would become the most closely studied record of her life.

pullQuote.text: For a while her songs were better known than she was.

sections.heading: Wild Columbine
paragraphs: The instrument that shaped those songs was not a guitar. At the Big Sur Folk Festival in 1969 Mitchell had come across the Appalachian dulcimer, the long, slim, fretted zither of the American mountains, and bought one from the luthier Joellen Lapidus for $200. Lapidus called it Wild Columbine, after the flower-like sound holes carved into its top. It was light enough to take anywhere, and most of what became *Blue* was written on it.

Strummed hard, a dulcimer drones and chimes at once, a bright, slightly nasal ring that sits somewhere between a back-porch folk instrument and a sitar. Mitchell played it the way she was by then playing guitar: percussively, with a slapping attack that David Yaffe hears as partly learned from Stephen Stills and yet entirely hers. It is the first sound on the album. [[All I Want]] opens on dulcimer chords that Yaffe compares to an engine starting, and then her voice comes in, restless and quick, turning over the question of what a love that leaves both people free might actually look like, and whether such a thing can exist at all.

sections.heading: The caves at Matala
paragraphs: The road led to Greece, and in early 1970 to Matala, a fishing village on the south coast of Crete where a few dozen young travellers had made homes in caves cut into the cliffs above the beach. There were two tavernas, a bakery, a couple of small shops and a single telephone. Mitchell stayed from the end of winter into the spring. She would later tell the *Wall Street Journal* that she spent those months with salt in her hair and tar on her feet, living about as roughly as she ever had.

In one of the tavernas she met Cary Raditz, an American from Winston-Salem, North Carolina, who had walked out of a copywriting job in 1969, hitchhiked to Greece and arrived in Matala that Halloween. He cooked at the Delfini and ran a small business making leather sandals. Over several weeks, in different corners of the village, Mitchell wrote [[Carey]] for him as a present for his April birthday. Raditz later described watching her work to the writer Marc Myers: “She’d go into a kind of trance, and things would come out of that.”

The finished song is a postcard with sand still in it, warm and loose, its dulcimer and drums lilting toward calypso. An earlier draft had been harder on its subject, and she rewrote it into something kinder. Under the holiday mood, she later admitted, she was still grieving the end of her relationship with Nash.

[[California]] is the same journey seen from the far end. Peter Kearns reads it as a diary entry, written in France as homesickness set in: a traveller moving between Paris and the Greek islands, reading grim news from Vietnam in the papers, and aching to be back on the West Coast among people who understood her. Raditz makes a brief, lightly disguised appearance. On the record, James Taylor’s guitar and the pedal steel of Sneaky Pete Kleinow, of the Flying Burrito Brothers, give it a loping, sunlit lift, as though the flight home had already begun its descent.

pullQuote.text: The finished song is a postcard with sand still in it

sections.heading: Older songs, deeper water
paragraphs: Not everything on *Blue* came from that year. [[Little Green]] is the oldest song on the record, written in 1966 and copyrighted in 1967, before her first album had been made. Listeners in 1971 had no way of knowing what it was about. In February 1965, at twenty-one and with almost no money, Mitchell had given birth to a daughter in Toronto and placed her for adoption. She kept that private for nearly thirty years. It became public in the 1990s, and in 1997 mother and daughter were reunited. Heard now, the song’s gentle lullaby, full of hopes for a child growing up somewhere else, carries a weight that was there all along, waiting to be understood.

[[My Old Man]] began as a lyric sketch in the spring of 1970, and Mitchell played an unfinished version on BBC television that September. It is the album’s happiest love song, a toast to a partnership that needs no marriage licence to be real, set to bright, jazz-tinged piano, though its later verses admit how quiet the house becomes when he is away. [[This Flight Tonight]] runs the other way: a song of second thoughts in mid-air, regretting a departure even as the plane climbs. Mitchell played it in a low open tuning that Kearns hears as almost a world-music drone, and Yaffe suggests its lover is a composite rather than any one person.

Toward the end of 1970 Mitchell played a Greenpeace benefit in Vancouver alongside James Taylor, with whom she was then involved. Both were going through hard times, and the relationship did not last. Yaffe writes that she came out of it with a batch of new songs, some darker than anything she had written before. Among the darkest is [[Blue]], a slow, nearly hymn-like piano piece addressed to someone who shares the album’s name, weighing up the many ways people of her generation were trying to numb themselves. Hinton hears it as a lullaby, though one sung to a hurt grown-up rather than a child.

pullQuote.text: carries a weight that was there all along, waiting to be understood

sections.heading: Lock the door
paragraphs: Mitchell recorded *Blue* at A&M Studios in Hollywood, where she had made her two previous albums, through the winter of 1970 and into early 1971, finishing in March. She produced it herself, with Henry Lewy, her engineer and close collaborator, at the desk. Down the corridor in Studio B, Carole King was making *Tapestry*. The atmosphere between the rooms was friendly, and Mitchell sang backing vocals on King’s record and on Taylor’s *Mud Slide Slim and the Blue Horizon*. The one point of contention was a red Steinway piano in Studio C. Both women wanted it, and Mitchell booked the room most often.

The sessions themselves were kept almost private. Looking back fifty years later in an interview with Cameron Crowe, Mitchell said she felt too exposed to have people watching her sing these songs, so Lewy locked the door. She remembered their partnership as warm and easy, more like family than work.

Only four other musicians appear. Stephen Stills plays bass and guitar on [[Carey]]. James Taylor plays acoustic guitar on [[All I Want]], [[California]] and [[A Case of You]]. Russ Kunkel adds drums to [[Carey]], [[California]] and [[A Case of You]], and Sneaky Pete brings his pedal steel to [[California]]. Taylor remembered sessions with nobody else in the room but the three of them, and Lewy’s steady guidance: “Henry Lewy had us keep it simple.” Playing against Mitchell’s spare dulcimer, he said, left him free to choose his own chords.

The rest is Mitchell alone, on dulcimer, guitar or that red Steinway. [[River]] is her and the piano, its opening figure a slow, minor-shaded turn on the melody of “Jingle Bells”. It is set at Christmas rather than about it: a song about wanting to escape, from a place, a season and the wreck of a relationship, while everyone around is celebrating. Hinton and Karen O’Brien have each called it the saddest of all Christmas songs, and it has since become a seasonal standard in its own right. [[A Case of You]] pairs Mitchell’s dulcimer with Taylor’s guitar and treats love as something between intoxication and communion, a thing drunk down and carried in the blood. Kearns points out that its last chord never quite comes home, which feels exactly right.

pullQuote.text: It is set at Christmas rather than about it

sections.heading: Changing the ending
paragraphs: *Blue* very nearly came out as a different record. An early running order sent to Reprise opened with [[Carey]] and closed with [[River]], and included two songs that would not make the final album: “Hunter” and “Urge for Going”, the song Tom Rush had recorded years before. Mitchell asked the label to halt the pressing. In their place went the last two songs she wrote for the album, which became its new first and last tracks: [[All I Want]] and [[The Last Time I Saw Richard]].

The change gave the album its shape. Instead of drifting in on a holiday song and out on a winter one, *Blue* now begins with a question about what love should be and ends with an old, unsentimental answer. [[The Last Time I Saw Richard]] is a piano ballad that looks back to her Detroit years in the mid-1960s, a late-night conversation in a bar with a cynical acquaintance who has given up on romance. O’Brien notes how it breaks the usual rules of songwriting and feels closer to a prose poem spoken aloud than to a song. It closes with the singer admitting that she is in a dark season of her own, but one she expects to come out of. After everything before it, that small promise lands like dawn.

The cover broke with habit too. Mitchell had painted or designed the sleeves of her first three albums. For *Blue*, under the art direction of Gary Burden, she used a photograph by Tim Considine: her face caught mid-song and flooded with deep blue. According to her archivist Joel Bernstein it was not a new picture at all, but one taken at the Troubadour in West Hollywood in 1967 or 1968.

pullQuote.text: After everything before it, that small promise lands like dawn.

sections.heading: No defences
paragraphs: Reprise released *Blue* on 22 June 1971. It reached number 15 in the United States, number 9 in Canada and number 3 in the United Kingdom. [[Carey]] went out as the first single in July, with [[This Flight Tonight]] on the B-side, and reached number 93 on the Billboard Hot 100. [[California]] followed in October, backed with [[A Case of You]].

Many critics understood at once what they were hearing. Robert Hilburn of the *Los Angeles Times* suggested it might be the best album of the year, and Robert Christgau ranked it her finest. But the frankness unsettled some of her peers. Kris Kristofferson is said to have urged her to keep something of herself back, and Mitchell later recalled male contemporaries warning her that no one would ever cover songs this personal.

She was wary of the label that critics soon reached for. She thought calling the songs confessional put the emphasis on the artist instead of the art, and she rejected comparisons with confessional poets such as Sylvia Plath and Anne Sexton. Yet she never pretended the album was guarded. Talking to Cameron Crowe for *Rolling Stone* in 1979, she said there was “hardly a dishonest note in the vocals,” and described how undefended she had felt at the time: “I felt like a cellophane wrapper on a pack of cigarettes.” The openness that had been so hard to live through was, she said, exactly what gave the music its strength.

pullQuote.text: She thought calling the songs confessional put the emphasis on the artist instead of the art

sections.heading: The long afterlife
paragraphs: The warning that nobody would sing these songs turned out to be spectacularly wrong. Nazareth turned [[This Flight Tonight]] into a hard-rock hit in 1973, reaching the UK top 20 and number one in Germany. [[A Case of You]] has been recorded by k.d. lang, Prince, Tori Amos and James Blake, among many others. [[River]] has become one of the most widely covered songs of its season, sung every December by people who may never have heard the rest of the album.

The record itself kept growing. It was certified platinum in the United States in 1986, and Yaffe reports that over time it overtook *Court and Spark* to become her best-selling album. In 2020 *Rolling Stone* placed it third in its list of the 500 greatest albums of all time, the highest position for a woman, and NPR’s survey of albums by women put it first. Musicians as different as Elton John, Taylor Swift and Haim have spoken of it as a touchstone, and Bob Dylan’s “Tangled Up in Blue” is often heard as a nod in its direction. For its fiftieth anniversary in 2021, Mitchell shared a set of previously unreleased demos and outtakes from the sessions.

What keeps people returning is not only the candour. It is the craft that holds the candour steady: the dulcimer that keeps time like a heartbeat, the piano that never decorates, the voice that leaps an octave and lands exactly where it meant to. *Blue* is short, a little over thirty-five minutes, and almost nothing on it is wasted. It was made in a locked room by someone who felt she had no skin, and it has spent half a century being let out, one listener at a time.

pullQuote.text: It was made in a locked room by someone who felt she had no skin
